Case study · UX research

Digital help research

Understand how people experience help in moments of need, and how digital help can best support them across meeting their goal.

Method

Semi-structured interviews

Participants

10+

Duration

60 mins each

Platform

usertesting.com

Research background

We’re looking to better grasp a shared, defined understanding of what ‘good help’ means that matches customers’ mental model, and how good help translates digitally.

Research objectives

  1. 01

    Gathering an understanding on what ‘Help’ vs. ‘Good Help’ vs. ‘Digital Help’ means to customers

  2. 02

    Gather signals from high-level concepts, and understand how it benchmarks against customers’ understanding of good help

  3. 03

    Explore how trust is built digitally

  4. 04

    Define what the role of AI and automation plays in getting help

The insights we’ve captured in this phase of research are foundational, not evaluative. They define how customers recognise help, and are insights to support how we shape what the future of digital help looks like.

Moments of need

Moments of need are driven by uncertainty, emotional load, and a need for reassurance, not just functional needs and technical failure.

It stopped working

I don’t understand what’s happening

Takeaway 1

People seek help to regain confidence, not just to fix a problem

Help is being looked for when things feel unclear, inconsistent, or are uncertain, not only when something has fully stopped working. When digital help jumps straight to diagnosis, it skips the moment customers are actually asking for reassurance and clarity.

People are initially self-serving on their own (checking FAQs, looking at online sources, online community forums etc.) before committing to a help path. Early help is about reassurance and validation before action.

Escalation (trying to speak to someone) happens when uncertainty remains, and self-serving becomes exhausting and too much effort. Self-serving shouldn’t feel like a lot of effort.

How might we ensure we restore confidence, not just diagnose or resolve?

How might we support sense-checking and reassurance before problem solving begins?

Takeaway 2

People seek human support for reassurance, not just because digital help lacks capability

Even when digital options and tools technically exist to support, the support can feel basic. People turn to humans for support, not because they can’t self-serve, but because escalating to a human can feel faster, people feel listened to, which supports the need for reassurance, empathy and confirmation.

It reassured me that it would get to a person to review it

Human agents are more accepted when it takes a while for them to solve, fix or address a concern. They’re valued even when they don’t fix instantly.

Assisted channels remain pivotal in help. Even when digital self-serve help is available, sometimes it’s not enough, and that doesn’t mean people won’t call… there needs to be a blended system, with a healthy balance, where nothing looks like a replacement.

Takeaway 3

When people seek help, they want to feel they’re moving forward, not starting again

  1. Step 1

    I have a need, question, or concern

  2. Step 2

    I want progress

  3. Step 3

    I want confidence I’m moving towards the right outcome

People navigate whatever path gives them the fastest, most confident progress toward an outcome.

Frequent frustrations when getting help

  • Need to repeat their situation across touchpoints
  • Being transferred with no context carried over or forward
  • Being directed to links or steps they’ve already tried or seen
  • Interactions felt like they were starting again

People want…

  • Their moment of need to follow them across touchpoints
  • Their effort to feel like it’s worthwhile
  • To feel heard, and confident the system understands their situation

How might we increase people’s confidence that they are on the right path to an outcome?

How might we make moving between help touchpoints feel like progress, not a reset?

Across the interviews, frustration wasn’t just about the existence of the digital help services, chatbots, or contact services, it was about losing progress and feeling like the system was not learning about their situation.

Takeaway 4

Good help can be recognised before resolution

People often highlighted positive aspects of getting help before reaching resolution:

  • People described feeling better once they understood what would happen next or where the issue derives from
  • Signs of feeling like they’re on the right track included: updates, explanations, clear next steps, confirmations and follow-ups
  • Follow-ups and confirmations were just as important as the outcomes

When people feel heard and know what’s happening next, confidence comes back even if the issue isn’t fixed yet.

How might we show clear signals that are important to feeling helped?

How might we show early reassurance, even when there’s no confirmed outcome yet?

Defining help

Defining ‘Help’ and ‘Digital Help’

These definitions reflect a shared understanding of help and digital help, shaped from participant interviews (not in the context of the provider or the provider’s experiences, but help in general).

Moments of need = help

  • Uncertainty

    Am I understanding this right?

  • Navigating

    Where do I start?

  • Sense checking

    Will this impact me?

  • Problem solving

    I think something is broken

  • Reassurance

    Has this been done right?

What does good help mean to customers?

Good help makes people feel reassured, understood, and not left guessing, restoring confidence when they feel uncertain.

  1. 01

    Good help restores confidence and reassurance

    • People don’t feel left guessing
    • Uncertainty and concerns are acknowledged
    • Clear understanding of what’s happening
  2. 02

    Good help makes people feel understood, not processed

    • Shows things are clearly being handled
    • Shows someone’s listening and understanding the need
  3. 03

    Good help provides clarity and guidance

    • Provides clear instructions
    • Makes next steps obvious
    • Takes ownership

Meeting emotional needs is just as important as meeting functional needs.

Customers often reference human support when describing “good help”, not because help must be human, but because humans most reliably deliver reassurance, understanding, and ownership.

Digital help must learn to signal these qualities just as clearly.

What does good help look like when it’s digital?

Digital help is a joined-up, low-effort experience that keeps customers informed, shows progress, and helps them understand what’s happening, so they can feel confident things are being handled.

  1. 01

    A unified, joined-up experience

    • Centralised hub / one system
    • Capabilities to transfer and direct to other modes of support/diagnostics seamlessly
  2. 02

    Minimal effort

    • Less emotional and cognitive effort
    • Ability to multi-task
    • Easy access to escalate
    • Proactively kept informed/live updates
  3. 03

    Clear handling

    • Kept informed, live updates/status updates
    • Signs of progress and handling
  4. 04

    Supports understanding

    • It guides, it directs, it instructs, it provides an outcome
    • Helps make sense of what’s happening
    • Provides info in an accessible way

Digital help must deliver the same confidence signals customers associate with human help through digital-native ways like updates, progress visibility, and joined-up journeys.

Digital help needs to show it can visibly handle complexity and context.

Key finding

Digital help fails not because customers expect too much, but because it fails to deliver the basic signals that make help feel “handled” or like their need is “understood”.

Where it fails

Where digital help is failing

Digital help needs to shift, so customers feel like they can get help digitally the way they do via traditional help (assisted channel) or speaking to a human.

Participants assume only humans can handle:

  • Unique or perceived complex problems
  • When you explain a need for help in an in-detail way
  • How they type responses (via chat)

Where digital help breaks

  • Generic FAQs, content and responses
  • Loop behaviour
  • Content / information overload
  • Poor chatbot UX (limited functionality, responses, not understanding context)
  • No visible access to escalated support channels (live agent support, call-up support etc.)

Trust, AI and automation

The role of trust, AI and automation

Trust is built through visibility and continuity, not tone and friendliness

Trust begins to decline when digital help feels performative. This includes:

  • When responses feel scripted or generic
  • When there’s no explanation why something is happening
  • When help “loops”
  • When escalation/assisted support feels hidden or blocked

People don’t decide they trust help because it feels nice or sounds friendly.

They trust it when they can see that something is happening and understand what’s going on.

What we’re learning so far that builds trust

Progress signals, updates, next steps, confirmations, follow-ups etc.

The role of AI in digital help

People are becoming more aware of AI’s presence, and its capabilities. AI is not a new type of help, it’s how help shows up, that can either strengthen or destroy trust.

AI is welcomed when it:
  • Reduces effort (admin, searching, summarising, triage)
  • Speeds things up for simple or known issues
  • Helps people understand information (sense-making, explaining)
  • Surfaces the right next steps
AI loses trust when it:
  • Pretends to understand but doesn’t
  • Gives confident but wrong answers
  • Doesn’t ask clarifying questions
  • Feels like a smarter FAQ, rather than adaptive help
  • Becomes a barrier to human support

This reinforces the concerns and frustrations when discussing experiences with chatbots and AI-based assistants.

AI should behave as a support system.

ChatGPT sets the bar for AI, anything less feels untrustworthy

People trust AI when it behaves like advanced Gen AI platforms such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or Copilot etc., where it allows you to push back and adapts as you add more context.

They lose trust when websites have generic AI assistants that feel scripted, limited, deflect, or just feel like smarter FAQs.

Company websites don’t use AI in the best way possible

People don’t dislike AI, but emotional connection comes from building a rapport/relationships, which is why AI works best as support, not the emotional face of help.

Digital help

How the provider should look to show up when customers need help

Digital help at the provider

Digital help at the provider defines how we show up when customers need help, this can make or break brand trust.

What digital help at the provider should be:

  • Joined-up
  • Informative
  • Adaptive
  • Transparent
  • Confidence building

What digital help should NOT be:

  • Purely transactional
  • Overly automated without visibility
  • Generic
  • Positioned as ‘AI-first’ at the cost of trust

It should make it easy for customers to understand what’s happening, what to do next, and whether they need to do anything at all.

Core principles

Digital help at the provider | Core principles

How might we design for these principles?

Remove uncertainty

Digital help must reduce uncertainty, not just provide answers

Research shows reassurance comes from visibility, not just tone or what someone says.

Customers don’t just want information, they want to know:

  • What’s happening
  • What’s been done
  • What will happen next

How might we prevent correct but confusing experiences that still lead customers to assisted support?

How might we ensure we don’t make customers feel like they’re stuck in loops without knowing why?

Unified experience

Digital help should feel like one joined-up system

Help is expected to carry context and hold the journey together.

Customers don’t think about tools or channels, they expect help to feel continuous, even if it moves between:

  • Content/FAQs
  • Diagnostics
  • Chat
  • Human support

How might we ensure our help services and systems are not fragmented, and are smooth transitions rather than hand-offs?

How might we show ownership even when help moves between systems or people?

How might we ensure we carry context, and don’t make customers feel like they’re starting again or going in a loop?

Make help light

Digital help must minimise effort in moments of need

People are coming to help already stressed, overwhelmed or uncertain, we need to make the experience feel stress-free.

Effort is more than time, it’s emotional and cognitive load. We want to make sure there are fewer decisions and things to think about at high-stress moments.

How might we ensure we present information and content in a way that doesn’t overload or overwhelm?

How might we reduce the thinking and guessing for customers in the moment of need?

How might we ensure we adapt help when understanding and confidence improves, but also prioritise speed?

Show the work

Digital help must be progressive

Trust comes from seeing something happen, and feeling like things are being acknowledged and handled.

Progress enhances trust, we see people feel confident when they can see:

  • Movement
  • Acknowledgement
  • Momentum

Not just outcomes.

How might we show there is movement happening even if it’s happening in the background?

How might we help customers see momentum, even when or if resolution takes time?

How might we show time is being used productively and effectively on the customer’s behalf?

Assistive, not authoritative

AI should support understanding and action

AI is being embraced on a frequent basis, even for day-to-day support. How AI supports and is presented needs to be well executed to be trusted.

  • AI that assists, not dominates
  • There needs to be transparency about what AI is doing
  • AI that knows when to step back or when it can’t support

How might we help AI guide customers without taking away their sense of control?

How might we ensure we use AI to support decision-making rather than making the decisions?

How might we make AI transparent about its confidence and limits?

Concepts

Appendix

We used early concepts to uncover how people think about help, what they expect to see, what reassures them, and where confidence breaks down

Concepts – concierge

  • Stepper

    Visual aid to show visible progress

  • Chatbot entry

    The chatbot’s identity is not recognised by customers, however it is associated as a support tool to use for help, often referenced as a chatbot

  • AI icon

    Icon widely associated with AI and as a secondary support tool for assistance

Takeaways

  • We saw participants latch onto the colour to provide status clarity (red banner suggests issue, green banner suggests no issue)
  • The opportunity to be kept informed was suggested to help build reassurance
  • Access to further assisted support (chat or phone) enhanced trust

Concepts – dashboard

  • Status chips

    Whilst colours support with visual aid, the use of blue caused confusion on what’s trying to be suggested

Takeaways

  • Access to further assisted support (chat or phone) continues to enhance trust
  • The use of seeing AI in help is becoming the norm
  • Quick links and help topics are seen to support with navigating this help and support concept

Concepts – chat interface

  • Search bar

    “Ask me anything” suggests it has a wide knowledge base, so there are high expectations for it to be an advanced tool to minimise effort

Takeaways

  • AI driving this concept feels like it’s a good starting point for self-serving, seen as a tool to find information quicker
  • Proactive and actionable conversational responses build up confidence
  • Questions raised around how ‘smart’ and ‘advanced’ the AI smart search would be (the continuous comparison to ChatGPT)
  • Access to further assisted support (chat or phone) continues to enhance trust

Co-creation

Live sketching helped translate participants’ mental models of digital help into visible signals in their own words

Help needs to signify known things… knowing if it’s an individual issue to the house

It should show guidance on how to use the AI conversational

I’d like it to ask me this question of how do I want results to be sort of presented

I want to refer back to my help, be able to ask for transcript or email follow-up for future reference

Empathy map

Empathy map

Pains
  • Difficult to immediately speak to a human (via live chat or phone call)
  • Self-serve content and services are not doing enough (lack of different formats)
  • Issue/question is not being resolved in first attempt
  • Poor customer service from live representative
Gains
  • Speaking to someone, they’re able to apologise and show tangible empathy
  • Being kept in the loop on the progress of the issue/problem
  • Able to be compensated or value gain based on need for help
